description: Choose correct grammar form: tense, preposition, modal, conjunction

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She has been working here ___ five years.'

options.option_text: Since, with a starting point
For, with a duration of time
From, with a starting point too
In, used at a fixed time only

questions.explanation: FOR = used with DURATION (period of time): for 5 years, for 2 hours, for a long time. SINCE = used with a STARTING POINT (specific moment in time): since 2020, since Monday, since I came. 'Five years' is a duration → use FOR. SSC PYQ favourite. Memory: 'For-Duration / Since-Starting-point'.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'If I ___ a millionaire, I would buy a yacht.'

options.option_text: Am, present-tense indicative form
Were, the subjunctive 'unreal' form
Will be, the future-tense form
Was, the past-tense form here

questions.explanation: SECOND CONDITIONAL (unreal/hypothetical present situation): If + past simple (or 'were' for all subjects), would + base. 'Were' is the SUBJUNCTIVE used for unreal conditions, even with I/he/she/it. 'If I were rich' (formal/correct) vs 'If I was rich' (colloquial). Other formulas: 1st CONDITIONAL (real future) = if + present, will + base ('If it rains, I will stay'). 3rd CONDITIONAL (unreal past) = if + had + V3, would have + V3.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'The book is ___ the table.'

options.option_text: In, used for inside an enclosed space
On, when contact with surface above
At, used for a precise location point
By, meaning beside or near to

questions.explanation: ON = surface contact (book ON table, picture ON wall, ring ON finger). IN = inside enclosed space (key IN drawer, water IN bottle). AT = at a specific point/place (at the bus stop, at home, at the door). BY = next to / near (sit by the window). All are PREPOSITIONS OF PLACE — most-tested in SSC + banking exams.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'Neither John ___ his brothers ___ available today.'

options.option_text: Or / are, the parallel form here used
Nor / are, agreeing with nearest subject
Nor / is, the singular verb form used
Or / is, the mixed standard form used

questions.explanation: NEITHER ... NOR (correlative pair). The verb agrees with the SUBJECT NEAREST to it (proximity rule). Here, 'his brothers' (plural) is nearest → 'are'. If reversed: 'Neither his brothers nor John IS available' (singular John nearest → 'is'). EITHER ... OR follows same rule. Distractor 1 — 'or' wrong (must be 'nor'). Distractor 3 — wrong agreement.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'I ___ rather stay at home tonight.'

options.option_text: Will, simple future tense form
Would, with 'rather' for preference
Should, expressing duty here
Could, expressing ability here

questions.explanation: 'WOULD RATHER' = expression of PREFERENCE. Followed by base verb (without 'to'). 'I would rather stay' = I prefer to stay. Same pattern: 'I had better leave' (had better + base). 'I'd rather not go' = preference not to. Cannot use 'will rather' or 'should rather' — these are wrong. Distractor 4 'could rather' also incorrect English.

questions.stem: Fill in: 'He works ___ a software engineer in Bangalore.'

options.option_text: Like a software engineer in Bangalore
As a software engineer in Bangalore
For a software engineer in Bangalore
On a software engineer in Bangalore

questions.explanation: AS = identity / role / profession ('he works AS an engineer' = he is one). LIKE = comparison ('he works LIKE a robot' = behaves similarly to one, but isn't one). LIKE/AS distinction is heavily tested. 'As' for jobs/roles ('appointed as captain'); 'like' for similes ('she runs LIKE a deer').

questions.stem: Fill in: 'Hardly had I entered the room ___ the lights went off.'

options.option_text: Then, used after a long pause
When, completing 'Hardly had ...'
Than, after comparative form
And, used for joining clauses

questions.explanation: Inverted pattern: HARDLY HAD ... WHEN ... = means one thing happened immediately followed by another. SCARCELY HAD ... WHEN ... (same construction). Compare: NO SOONER HAD ... THAN ... (uses 'than', not 'when'). 'No sooner had I entered THAN the lights went off.' Strict pairing: hardly/scarcely → when; no sooner → than. Common SSC trap: testing 'hardly...than' (wrong) or 'no sooner...when' (wrong).
